title: The Whole Routine
description: Five stages from shuffle to recall, a palace big enough for a deck, and why champions review backwards

concepts.title: How it works: five stages, one deck
concepts.contentHtml:
Someone slaps a freshly shuffled deck on the table and starts a stopwatch. This is the moment the whole course has been building towards, and the good news is that most of the work is already done. Memorising a deck is not one feat but five stages, and two of them happen before you ever see the cards.

A 2023 paper written with the memory athlete Nelson Dellis, who reached grandmaster ranking at the 2012 World Memory Championships,1 spells out the champions' routine. Long before a competition, the palace and the person-action-object list are fixed and learned by heart.2 Dellis's own palace is his old high school, with stops such as the entrance, particular classrooms and the gymnasium.3 On the day, the cards go in three at a time, one scene per place. When the last scene is down, Dellis stops his timer and uses the remaining time to review the palace.4 Then he walks the route in order and turns each scene back into three cards. Dellis's own time in the paper is 40.65 seconds for a whole deck.5

  • Images ready: your 52 faces, actions and objects from A Face for Every Card.
  • A palace big enough: 52 places at one card each, 26 at two, or 18 with PAO.
  • Memorise: three cards, one scene, next place.
  • Review: one pass back through the palace before you recall.
  • Recall: walk the route and decode every scene.

Notice the split. The first two stages are homework you do once; the last three are what you practise, again and again. Nothing about the system is decided at the table, which is exactly why it can be fast.

concepts.title: Drill: a palace for the deck
concepts.contentHtml:
Your first palaces held ten or twelve things. A deck needs more room, so build its palace now, before a single card comes out. The arithmetic from A Face for Every Card decides the size.

  1. Choose your format. One face per place needs 52 places, and two faces meeting in each place need 26. PAO needs 18: seventeen scenes, with the last card alone on place 18 or worked out by elimination. If your actions and objects are not instant yet, start with two faces a place and switch later.
  2. Join routes if you must. Few homes hold 18 good places. Run your home route straight into your outdoor route from Your First Palace, always in the same direction.
  3. Mark the fives. A golden hand on place 5, Decimus on place 10, and so on. With PAO, place 5 holds cards 13 to 15 and place 10 holds cards 28 to 30, so the markers double as a card counter.
  4. Walk it until it bores you, forwards and backwards, naming every place aloud.
  5. Load and review backwards. Put the drill below on places 1 to 4, then walk from place 4 back to place 1 before you recall, the way Dellis reviews.
Drill Twelve cards make four PAO scenes on places 1 to 4 (or use twelve places, one face each). Review backwards, then recall. The quiz will ask for them.
  1. 2 of spades
  2. 5 of clubs
  3. 4 of clubs
  4. ace of hearts
  5. 4 of diamonds
  6. 8 of hearts
  7. queen of spades
  8. 7 of diamonds
  9. ace of diamonds
  10. 6 of diamonds
  11. 5 of spades
  12. 7 of spades

Scene one, to start you off: Snow White hugging a string of prayer beads on your doormat. Build the other three yourself, and make each one move.

concepts.title: Myth check: one look and done
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Champions see the deck once and it is fixed; reviewing is for beginners.
Reality Dellis reviews every time, and he does it backwards. He traverses the palace from the most recent spot to the first,1 and he reports that this review is crucial. Once he has been through it a single time, he finds he can think about something else, or even hold a conversation, for the rest of the time and still recall the cards.2 The review is not a nervous check. It is the stage that seals the deck in.
Myth Once a deck is memorised, it stays memorised.
Reality Not without help, and in competition nobody wants it to. Days after Joshua Foer won the USA Memory Championship in 2006, he explained on NPR that competitors actually want to forget everything as soon as possible afterwards, to be ready for the next event.3 If you wanted to store it for longer, he said, you would repeat it to yourself maybe once or twice and it would stick.4

Wait, really? Foer's "once or twice" is the spacing effect from How Memory Works in disguise. A deck you want to keep for a week needs a few reviews spread out to match that wait, the way the review plan in that skill spaced them. A deck you want gone should simply be left alone, so its scenes fade and the palace is clear for the next one. So every finished deck asks you a question: keep it, or let it go? Your answer decides whether you walk the palace again tomorrow.

tryIt: Build your deck palace: choose 18 places (26 if you will use two faces a place), mark every fifth one, and walk the route forwards and backwards twice without a slip.

title: Speed and Accuracy
description: The speed-accuracy trade-off, training in stages of 13, 26 and 52 cards, and an error log that shows what to fix

concepts.title: How it works: the oldest trade-off
concepts.contentHtml:
Deal ten cards and name each face aloud as fast as you can. Now do it again, twice as fast. Somewhere in the second run a rock star turns into a geek, and you have met one of the most reliable effects in psychology.

It is called the speed-accuracy trade-off. A 2014 review by Richard Heitz of Vanderbilt University opens with its reach: from insects to rodents to primates, faster decisions tend to be less accurate ones.1 The idea is older than most famous experiments. In 1899 R. S. Woodworth's dissertation showed that the accuracy of an action varies with its speed. In 1911 Henmon gave people two lines that differed slightly in length and asked which was longer;2 when he sorted the answers by how long they took, speed and accuracy were plainly linked. In 1922 H. E. Garrett replicated the finding and gave it a name, the speed-accuracy relation.3

For you the lesson is practical. You do not get fast by trying to be fast. You get fast by being accurate at a pace a little above comfortable, again and again, until that pace feels easy and the next one beckons. Push too far and the errors pile up; stay too safe and you learn little. So this skill's rule is accuracy first, then speed, and the drill below gives you two tools for it: stages you may only climb when you are clean, and an error log that shows exactly where accuracy breaks when you push. As the myth check shows, memory sport's own scoring makes the same demand.

concepts.title: Drill: thirteen, twenty-six, fifty-two
concepts.contentHtml:
Here is the training plan for the rest of the skill. It climbs through a quarter, a half and then the whole deck, and it keeps a written record of every slip, because a mistake you can see is a mistake you can fix.

  1. Stage one: 13 cards. Shuffle, take the top 13, start the stopwatch and memorise them: four PAO scenes and one lone card on place 5. Stop the watch, review backwards, then write the order down or lay it out with a second deck.
  2. Climb only when clean. This course's rule: two perfect runs in a row at one stage earn the next, 26 cards and then all 52. A mistake means another run at the same stage.
  3. Log every error. Write the position, what you recalled, what was really there and the type: a blank (an empty place), a swap (right value, wrong suit, or the reverse), an order slip (right cards, wrong places) or a decode slip (right image, turned into the wrong card).
  4. Fix the pattern, not the slip. A card that turns up twice in the log gets a new face or a sharper action. A place that keeps going blank gets moved or replaced.
  5. Then shave seconds. Once a stage is clean, aim to beat your best time by a few seconds. If errors return, slow down until they stop.
Drill A first timed set: memorise these twelve as four scenes against a stopwatch, recall them, and log any errors. The quiz will ask for them.
  1. 7 of diamonds
  2. ace of clubs
  3. 10 of clubs
  4. 9 of spades
  5. 7 of hearts
  6. 5 of clubs
  7. 2 of hearts
  8. 5 of diamonds
  9. 10 of diamonds
  10. jack of hearts
  11. jack of diamonds
  12. 7 of clubs

Keep the log in the deck box. Within a fortnight it will tell you more about your memory than any single score.

concepts.title: Myth check: only the clock counts
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth In memory sport, the fastest memoriser wins, full stop.
Reality Only with a perfect deck. As the 2023 Dellis paper sets out the World Memory Sports Council's rules, competitors get up to five minutes to memorise a shuffled deck, then rebuild its order with a second deck. If anyone gets the whole deck right, the winner is whoever memorised fastest, and the time spent rebuilding does not count.1 If every deck has a mistake, a judge compares the decks one card at a time, and your score is the number of correct cards before the first mistake.2 A lightning deck with a slip at card 4 scores 3.

Wait, really? Champion pace depends on how much there is to hold. Guinness World Records lists Zou Lujian's 13.96 seconds for one deck, set at the 2017 World Memory Championships in Shenzhen, China:3 about a quarter of a second per card. Its record for the most cards memorised in 30 minutes, 1,100 by Wei Qinru of China in Kuala Lumpur in 2019, works out at about 1.6 seconds per card, six times slower. The longer the event, the more speed the best in the world trade for accuracy. Your own times for 13, 26 and 52 cards will tell the same story in miniature.

tryIt: Memorise the top 13 cards of a shuffled deck against a stopwatch, check them, and start your error log with every slip and its type.

title: Memory Sport
description: The World Memory Championships, Dominic O'Brien, a journalist's 2006 win and whose records to trust

concepts.title: How it works: a sport is invented
concepts.contentHtml:
Imagine a sport whose athletes sit perfectly still, stare at cards and numbers, and now and then close their eyes. It has world rankings, grandmasters and a world champion, and it is only a few decades old.

According to the championships' own history, the mind sport of memory was founded in the UK by Tony Buzan, famous for Mind Mapping, and the chess grandmaster Raymond Keene.1 The two staged the first World Memory Championships in 1991.2 By 2015 the organisers counted some 35 countries taking part, competing over ten disciplines.3 The events test exactly what this course has trained. When Joshua Foer described them on NPR in 2006, he listed faces with names, lists of random words, numbers, and the order of a shuffled deck of playing cards.4

The first world champion was Dominic O'Brien, whose Dominic System you met in A Face for Every Card. He went on to take the title seven more times, eight in all.5 A University of Michigan page on dyslexia notes that the Guinness Book of World Records for 2002 listed him for repeating a random sequence of 54 decks, 2,808 cards, after looking at each card only once.6 Handle that figure with care: it is a university web page quoting a printed record book, not a record page you can check today. Asking where a number comes from is part of the sport, as the myth check below shows.

concepts.title: Drill: a Speed Cards heat at home
concepts.contentHtml:
You do not need a championship to compete. You need two decks, a stopwatch and ten minutes, and you can run a heat under championship rules at the kitchen table.

  1. Set up two decks. Shuffle one at least seven times, as A Face for Every Card advised. Put the other in factory order, ready for rebuilding.
  2. Memorise against the clock. Start the stopwatch, memorise, and stop it the moment you put the deck face down. Guinness's rules allow a maximum of five minutes,1 and you may spend whatever is left reviewing in your head, as Dellis does.
  3. Rebuild. When the five minutes are up, lay out the second deck in the order you memorised. Guinness allows another five minutes for this, and under memory sport's rules the rebuilding time does not count.
  4. Judge it. Turn the two decks over side by side, one card at a time. A perfect deck scores your memorising time. Otherwise your score is the number of correct cards before the first mistake.
  5. Log it. Time, score and every error go in your error log, each with its type.

Start your heats with 13 or 26 cards under the same rules, and move to the full deck when the stages from lesson 2 say you are ready. Do not measure yourself against the record books yet. Your first heat is a baseline, not a verdict, and the only competitor who matters this month is the person who ran yesterday's heat. Beat that person by a card or a second, and log how you did it.

concepts.title: Myth check: the record is the record
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth There is one world record for memorising a deck, and everyone agrees on it.
Reality It depends on who keeps the book. Guinness World Records, checked on 1 November 2026, lists 13.96 seconds by Zou Lujian of China, set at the 2017 World Memory Championships in Shenzhen on 8 December 2017.1 The 2023 paper written with Nelson Dellis instead names Shijir-Erdene Bat-Enkh as the Speed Cards world record holder, with a perfect deck in 12.74 seconds,2 but gives no date or event, and this course could not confirm it from a record body. So treat 13.96 seconds as verified by Guinness and 12.74 seconds as reported. A record without a source and a date is only a rumour.
Myth Memory champions are born with extraordinary memories.
Reality Joshua Foer, a science journalist, covered the contest the year before for Slate.3 The competitors told him they did not have extraordinary memories, they just knew tricks,4 and that even he could be champion if he learned them and practised. He tested the claim, beat five other contestants and won the 2006 USA Memory Championship.5 His deck took about a minute and 40 seconds, a new US record by his own account, while he said the best in the world could do it in under 30 seconds.6

Wait, really? The sport began as a protest. Buzan and Keene, the championships' history says, were frustrated that best-selling record books celebrated people who could eat the most Smarties in three minutes with chopsticks, or wear the most socks on one foot,7 while ignoring mental athletes. So they gave the mind a sport of its own, with rules, judges and record books. It is a fitting origin for the event you are training for: the whole point is that the feat can be checked.

tryIt: Run a home Speed Cards heat with 26 cards: memorise against a stopwatch with a five-minute cap, rebuild the order from a second deck, and score the cards right up to the first mistake.

title: Made, Not Born
description: Deliberate practice, what the champions' brains show, and how much practice really explains

concepts.title: How it works: the violinists of West Berlin
concepts.contentHtml:
Watch a champion memorise a deck in under a minute and the obvious thought is: I could never do that. Is it true? In 1993 the psychologist K. Anders Ericsson and his colleagues Ralf Krampe and Clemens Tesch-Römer went looking for an answer in a music school. They recruited three groups of ten violin students from the Music Academy of West Berlin:1 the best, nominated by their professors as potential international soloists, a good group, and a group heading for careers as music teachers. Each student estimated how much they had practised over the years and kept a diary for a week.

The estimates lined up with skill, and the authors drew a bold conclusion: individual differences in ultimate performance can largely be accounted for by differential amounts of past and current levels of practice.2 Apart from height and body size in some sports, they wrote, "we reject any important role for innate ability3". The kind of practice mattered too. They called it deliberate practice, and Ericsson and a colleague later described it as focused, effortful work aimed at improving: well-defined tasks at the right level of difficulty, with informative feedback to monitor progress,4 designed by a teacher or by the performers themselves.

Memory sport fits this picture unusually well. You met two studies of it in Your First Palace: Maguire's champions, who had no special brain structure, and Dresler's novices, who more than doubled their scores in six weeks. Dresler's team summed up the field in one line: such memory skills do not seem to be associated with extraordinary brain anatomy or general cognitive superiority, but are acquired through deliberate training.5 Their comparison was a stern one. To match the athletes' generally high intellectual level, some control volunteers were recruited from gifted students and members of Mensa,6 and the athletes still remembered far more.

concepts.title: Drill: practise the weak spots
concepts.contentHtml:
Dresler's study holds a quiet warning for anyone who has read this far: knowing the method is not the same as training it. His team compared their trainees with 18 men from another study who had taken only a two-day introductory course in the method of loci.1 Those men knew the principles just as well, but their brain networks showed none of the shift towards the athletes' pattern. The trainees' best scores for memorising random words in five minutes, meanwhile, climbed steadily over the six weeks, from 16.6 to 42.3.2

Deliberate practice means aiming that kind of training at your weakest point, and your error log already knows where it is.

  1. Find the repeat offenders. Read your log and list the cards, places and swaps that turn up more than once.
  2. Isolate them. Drill just those cards, first as flashcards and then in scenes, at a pace a little faster than comfortable.
  3. Check at once. Check after every run, not at the end of the session, so you never rehearse a wrong answer.
  4. Put them back. Shuffle the mended cards into ordinary 13-card runs and see whether they hold.
  5. Repeat weekly. A shrinking log is your progress chart.
Drill The trap: twelve cards built from only threes, sixes and nines, so every card has lookalikes. Memorise them as four scenes, then check for swaps. The quiz will ask for them.
  1. 9 of clubs
  2. 3 of hearts
  3. 9 of spades
  4. 9 of hearts
  5. 6 of diamonds
  6. 3 of spades
  7. 9 of diamonds
  8. 6 of clubs
  9. 6 of hearts
  10. 3 of diamonds
  11. 6 of spades
  12. 3 of clubs

concepts.title: Myth check: ten thousand hours
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Ten thousand hours of practice will make anyone an expert.
Reality The "10,000 hour rule" was made famous by Malcolm Gladwell's book Outliers,1 drawing on Ericsson's work, and it is tidier than the evidence. In 2019 Brooke Macnamara and Megha Maitra repeated the violin study's method with a double-blind procedure. They did not replicate its core finding that accumulated practice corresponded to each skill level:2 by age 20, both their best and their good violinists had averaged more than 10,000 hours of practice alone.3 Practice alone explained 26 per cent of the differences in performance,4 against 48 per cent in the original study's analysis. A 2014 meta-analysis led by Macnamara found that deliberate practice explained 26 per cent of the variance in performance for games, 21 per cent for music, 18 per cent for sports, 4 per cent for education and less than 1 per cent for professions.

Both sides deserve a fair hearing. The critics do not say practice is useless: explaining a quarter of performance, the replication's authors write, is not an inconsequential amount, and the meta-analysis concluded that deliberate practice is important, but not as important as has been argued. The argument is over how much practice explains, not whether it helps.

Wait, really? Dominic O'Brien, eight times world champion, was diagnosed with dyslexia as a student and found reading and writing hard. The University of Michigan's dyslexia project reports that he does not believe it held him back, and that he believes anyone can do what he does with proper training.5 That is one champion's belief, not a finding; but for memory sport, the brain studies above point the same way.

tryIt: Pick the five cards that turn up most in your error log, sharpen each one's face or action, and drill only those five for ten minutes.

title: The Whole Deck
description: What memory training will and will not do for you, then the finale: a whole shuffled deck in three stages

concepts.title: How it works: what transfers, and what does not
concepts.contentHtml:
Before the finale, an honest word about what you are about to become. You will be someone who can memorise a deck of cards. Will you also be smarter, sharper and safer from forgetting? The evidence says no, and it is worth knowing why.

In 2014 two groups of scientists published rival open letters about brain games. More than 70 scientists said such games offer no scientifically grounded way to improve thinking or stave off cognitive decline; months later, 133 scientists and practitioners replied that the literature is full of benefits. In 2016 Daniel Simons and six colleagues reviewed every peer-reviewed intervention study cited by leading brain-training companies. They found extensive evidence that training improves performance on the trained tasks, less evidence for closely related tasks, and little for distantly related tasks or everyday thinking. Many studies had major flaws in design or analysis, and none met all of the review's standards.

One of the biggest tests came from British television. Viewers of the BBC's Bang Goes The Theory were invited into a six-week online study, published in Nature in 2010 by Owen and colleagues. Of 52,617 people aged 18 to 60 who signed up, 11,430 took both the before and after tests, having trained for at least ten minutes a day, three times a week. They improved on every task they trained, yet showed no transfer to untrained tasks, even closely related ones.

Your deck skill works the same way. SF's digit training, in Numbers into Words, never touched his memory for letters, and Dresler's n-back trainees did no better at word lists than people who did nothing. A memory palace is a powerful tool you carry, not an upgrade to the machine.

concepts.title: Drill: the finale
concepts.contentHtml:
This is it: the whole deck. Do it in three stages, on three different days if you like, and do not move up until the stage below is clean.

  1. Warm up. Flip through the deck saying each face aloud, as in A Face for Every Card, and set aside any card that makes you hesitate.
  2. Stage one: 13 cards on 5 places. Four scenes and a lone card. Stop the watch, review backwards, rebuild with a second deck, judge, log.
  3. Stage two: 26 cards on 9 places. Eight scenes, then a person and an action sharing place 9. Same routine.
  4. Stage three: 52 cards on 18 places. Seventeen scenes and the last card alone on place 18, or worked out by elimination. Review backwards from 18 to 1, then rebuild the deck.
  5. Keep it, or let it go. To keep the deck, walk the palace again an hour later and the next day. To reuse the palace, leave it alone for a few days so the old scenes fade.
Drill Dress rehearsal: twelve cards, four scenes, the full routine with a stopwatch. The quiz will ask for them.
  1. jack of clubs
  2. 10 of spades
  3. queen of hearts
  4. 10 of diamonds
  5. 3 of spades
  6. king of hearts
  7. 7 of diamonds
  8. queen of spades
  9. 10 of hearts
  10. 6 of spades
  11. 4 of hearts
  12. king of clubs

When stage three comes back clean, write down the date and your time. You have memorised a shuffled deck of cards, which is exactly what this course promised at the start.

concepts.title: Myth check: a shield against dementia
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Memory training and brain games protect you against dementia.
Reality No technique in this course has been shown to prevent or treat dementia, and regulators have acted against companies that implied otherwise. In January 2016 the makers of the Lumosity brain-training program settled US Federal Trade Commission charges that they had deceived consumers with unfounded claims,1 including that their games could delay decline with age. The order imposed a $50 million judgment, suspended after the company paid $2 million.2 In the words of the FTC's Jessica Rich, Lumosity preyed on consumers' fears about age-related cognitive decline,3 suggesting its games could stave off memory loss, dementia and even Alzheimer's disease. If your memory worries you, talk to a doctor.
Myth A memory champion never loses their keys.
Reality Asked on NPR, days after winning the 2006 US championship, whether he was one of those people who remember where their car keys are, Joshua Foer said no: he was the person who shampoos his hair twice in the morning because he forgot he had just done it.4 The techniques worked on what he trained them on.

Wait, really? In the BBC study, the control group did not play brain games at all. They answered obscure questions in six categories, looking them up online. The authors concluded that six weeks of regular computerised brain training confers no greater benefit than simply answering general knowledge questions using the internet. So enjoy your new skill for what it is: a feat with more than 2,000 years of history behind it, a sport if you want one, and proof that a memory can be trained.

tryIt: Shuffle a real deck seven times, memorise all 52 cards in your deck palace, then rebuild the order with a second deck and count how many you got right before the first mistake.
